title: Prevalence of Schistosoma mansoni infection among children in Ethiopia: a systematic review and meta-analysis

subsections.subsection_title: Global and National Importance of Schistosomiasis
subsections.content:
Schistosomiasis remains one of the most important neglected tropical diseases globally and is disproportionately concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa, where it contributes substantially to chronic morbidity, disability, impaired child development, and reduced productivity in poor rural communities ref [1], ref [2], ref [3]. The disease is caused predominantly by Schistosoma mansoni and S. haematobium in Africa, and school-aged children bear a particularly heavy share of infection and morbidity because of intense and repeated water contact during daily domestic, recreational, and livelihood-related activities ref [1], ref [4].

The global significance of schistosomiasis extends beyond case counts to its broader developmental consequences. Chronic infection is associated with anemia, undernutrition, poor physical fitness, impaired cognition and educational performance, and long-term hepatointestinal or urogenital complications, reinforcing the well-described cycle between parasitic disease and poverty ref [1], ref [4], ref [5]. Despite advances in preventive chemotherapy, the disease continues to rank among the most consequential helminthiases in endemic regions, and Africa still accounts for the overwhelming majority of the global burden ref [2], ref [3].

Within Ethiopia, schistosomiasis is a major component of the national neglected tropical disease burden. National reviews have estimated that about 5.01 million people are infected and roughly 37.5 million live at risk, underscoring the importance of sustained surveillance and control ref [3]. Ethiopia is therefore a priority setting for intestinal schistosomiasis research, particularly because historical surveys documented wide spatial heterogeneity, with community-level S. mansoni prevalence ranging from low transmission to hyperendemic levels ref [3], ref [6]. This combination of high population at risk, focal transmission, and concentration of disease among children provides the central rationale for synthesizing evidence on S. mansoni prevalence in Ethiopian pediatric populations.

The policy architecture for schistosomiasis control has been shaped by the 2001 World Health Assembly Resolution 54.19, which repositioned schistosomiasis as a major public-health priority and endorsed large-scale preventive chemotherapy, particularly regular praziquantel treatment for school-aged children in endemic settings ref [4]. This framework was later broadened through WHO preventive chemotherapy guidance, which promoted integrated delivery platforms for schistosomiasis and other helminthiases while retaining school-aged children as the principal operational target group ref [4].

Over time, however, the policy discourse has shifted from morbidity control alone toward transmission reduction and eventual elimination. Contemporary analyses argue that reliance on annual mass drug administration, especially when coverage, compliance, and post-treatment reinfection remain suboptimal, is unlikely to achieve durable interruption of transmission without complementary interventions such as snail control, water, sanitation and hygiene, health education, and stronger local implementation systems ref [3], ref [5]. Thus, elimination is increasingly framed not as a pharmaceutical endpoint, but as a systems objective requiring multisectoral coordination and sustained financing ref [3], ref [4].

In Ethiopia, this rationale has been operationalized through the national schistosomiasis and soil-transmitted helminth control programme, which has expanded mapping, school-based deworming, and partner-supported delivery while also recognizing persistent gaps in treatment reach, surveillance, and integrated environmental control ref [5]. For Ethiopian children, especially those living in persistent transmission foci, the elimination agenda therefore provides a strong justification for synthesizing prevalence evidence: pooled estimates are needed to guide prioritization, assess progress beyond programmatic coverage metrics, and identify where intensified, locally adapted control strategies remain necessary ref [5], ref [3].

Ethiopia has a heterogeneous but substantial burden of intestinal schistosomiasis, with Schistosoma mansoni documented across most major regions and ecological zones. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis estimated a pooled national prevalence of 18.0%, while also showing marked between-study and between-region variability, underscoring that national averages obscure important local hotspots ref [6]. This spatial heterogeneity is consistent with the country’s long-recognized status as one of the higher-burden settings for helminthiases in sub-Saharan Africa, where transmission persists despite repeated preventive chemotherapy in many areas ref [6].

Available evidence indicates that geographic distribution is strongly structured by region and environment. In the meta-analysis, higher pooled prevalence was reported from southern Ethiopia, followed by Tigray and Oromia, while lower prevalence was observed in Harari and Afar ref [6]. The most comprehensive national mapping survey, based on more than 153,000 school-aged children in 625 woredas, further refined this picture: S. mansoni prevalence was concentrated mainly in western, northwestern, northern, and some south-central areas, whereas S. haematobium was largely restricted to lowland eastern foci, especially Somali and parts of Afar ref [4]. At woreda level, 67 districts were classified as endemic and 8 as highly endemic for schistosomes, highlighting the focal nature of transmission and the need for geographically targeted control ref [4].

Regional studies illustrate this micro-epidemiological patchiness. In Amhara, a population-based survey of 15,455 children found an overall S. mansoni prevalence of 6.9%, but zonal estimates ranged from 0.5% in Wag Hemra to 40.1% in Oromiya Zone, with district-level variation sufficient to alter treatment recommendations ref [8]. Such patterns reflect Ethiopia’s dependence on specific freshwater ecologies that support Biomphalaria hosts, together with altitude, irrigation, and river-lake systems that create highly focal transmission corridors rather than a uniform national distribution ref [4].

subsections.subsection_title: Local Transmission Patterns and Risk Factors in School-Aged Children
subsections.content:
Among Ethiopian school-aged children, transmission is highly localized and tightly linked to routine freshwater contact. Studies from Sanja, Jimma, and rural Bahir Dar consistently identify swimming, bathing, washing clothes or utensils, crossing rivers barefoot, fishing, and irrigation-related exposure as major determinants of infection, underscoring how domestic, recreational, and livelihood activities converge around cercaria-infested water bodies in both rural and urban settings ref [10], ref [12], ref [9], ref [10].

These exposure patterns help explain marked heterogeneity in prevalence between nearby communities and schools. Extremely high transmission has been documented in Sanja, where repeated river contact was strongly associated with infection, while moderate but still important burdens were reported in river-adjacent schools in Jimma and focal transmission sites such as Hayk ref [10], ref [12], ref [10], ref [11]. In Waja-Timuga, prevalence and mean egg counts peaked in late childhood and adolescence, supporting the typical pattern of intensified exposure during the second decade of life ref [8]. Several studies also report higher infection in boys, likely reflecting greater participation in swimming, irrigation, and other outdoor water-contact behaviors, although this sex gradient is not universal across settings ref [12], ref [8], ref [9].

Risk is further amplified where ecological modification sustains snail habitats, including irrigation schemes and estate agriculture. In Fincha’a sugar estate, S. mansoni infection co-occurred with substantial undernutrition, highlighting that repeated exposure among school-aged children has consequences beyond infection prevalence alone and may interact with broader social vulnerability ref [13]. Taken together, the Ethiopian literature indicates that school-age risk is driven less by age per se than by patterned contact with specific transmission sites and the social organization of children’s daily activities ref [10], ref [12], ref [8], ref [13].

subsections.subsection_title: Diagnostic and Mapping Considerations for Control Programs
subsections.content:
Diagnostic choice strongly influences both prevalence estimates and the programmatic classification of endemicity in schistosomiasis control. In Ethiopia, large-scale mapping has relied mainly on stool microscopy, especially the Kato-Katz technique, because it is inexpensive and operationally feasible in field settings; however, its sensitivity declines markedly in low-intensity infections, which become increasingly common after repeated praziquantel distribution. This creates a risk of underestimating residual transmission foci and misclassifying districts near treatment thresholds [1], ref [17], ref [3].

Evidence from the Ethiopian mapping context also shows that alternative examination strategies involve important trade-offs. During the national mapping platform, pooled stool examination substantially reduced laboratory time, but it had much lower sensitivity for detecting Schistosoma mansoni than individual examination, especially when infection intensity was light; consequently, pooling may be more suitable for rapid intensity appraisal than for prevalence-based treatment decisions [1]. These findings are consistent with broader guidance that mapping and monitoring tools should be selected according to program phase, transmission intensity, and the specific decision they are intended to support [2], ref [4].

For control programs, this implies that diagnostic and spatial mapping strategies should be interpreted together rather than separately. WHO guidance emphasizes subdistrict targeting, periodic remapping, and the use of fit-for-purpose diagnostics for monitoring progress toward elimination as a public health problem [2], ref [5]. In Ethiopia, where transmission is highly focal around water bodies and irrigation schemes, insensitive diagnostics can obscure micro-geographic heterogeneity; hence, strengthened sampling designs, georeferenced school surveys, and—where resources allow—more sensitive assays or repeated sampling are important to refine treatment allocation and post-MDA surveillance [3], ref [6].

subsections.subsection_title: Systematic Review Design for Observational Evidence
subsections.content:
This review was designed as a systematic synthesis of observational epidemiological evidence reporting the prevalence of Schistosoma mansoni among children in Ethiopia. For prevalence questions, methodological guidance recommends a review structure analogous to intervention reviews, but adapted to descriptive data, with an a priori protocol, explicit eligibility criteria, reproducible searching, formal appraisal, and transparent synthesis ref [18], ref [2]. Because the target parameter is prevalence rather than effect size, the review question is most appropriately framed using the CoCoPop approach—condition, context, and population—rather than PICO ref [18].

Accordingly, the population was defined as children in Ethiopia, typically school-age or preschool-age groups when explicitly reported; the condition was parasitologically confirmed S. mansoni infection; and the context comprised Ethiopian community- or school-based settings across regions and survey periods ref [18]. In prevalence reviews, cross-sectional studies using probability-based or otherwise clearly described sampling frames are generally the most directly relevant designs, although other observational surveys may be retained when they provide usable denominator-based estimates and align with the review objective ref [18], ref [3].

A key design feature for observational prevalence reviews is explicit evaluation of methodological quality. The Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and checklist emphasize assessment of sample-frame appropriateness, sampling strategy, adequacy of sample size, validity and consistency of outcome measurement, completeness of analytic coverage, and management of non-response ref [18], ref [4]. These domains are especially important in schistosomiasis surveys, where prevalence estimates are highly sensitive to population selection and diagnostic ascertainment. For reporting and conduct, alignment with broader standards for systematic reviews and meta-analyses, including protocol-based methods and transparent study selection, further strengthens reproducibility and interpretability ref [2], ref [5].

Assessment of statistical heterogeneity is central in prevalence meta-analysis because differences across Ethiopian studies may arise from geography, diagnostic approach, age structure, transmission ecology, and study execution. In practice, heterogeneity should first be examined using Cochran’s Q, but interpretation should not rely on the significance test alone because Q is strongly influenced by the number of included studies and has low power when meta-analyses contain few studies [1, 2].

Accordingly, heterogeneity is more informatively summarized with the I² statistic, which expresses the proportion of total observed variance attributable to real between-study differences rather than sampling error, together with an estimate of between-study variance (tau-squared, τ²) [1, 3]. Higgins and Thompson showed that I² and the related H statistic are less dependent on study count than Q and are therefore preferable descriptive measures in published meta-analyses [1]. For prevalence syntheses, where extreme proportions and variance instability are common, τ² remains important because it quantifies the absolute dispersion in underlying effects even when I² is high by construction [3, 4].

In systematic reviews of Schistosoma mansoni prevalence among Ethiopian children, substantial heterogeneity is expected a priori; thus interpretation should combine numerical indices with clinical and methodological appraisal. Conventional I² thresholds may be used only as rough heuristics, while subgroup analysis and meta-regression are needed to explore sources such as region, school versus community sampling, diagnostic technique, and study period [1, 2, 5]. When heterogeneity remains considerable, pooled estimates should be presented cautiously, preferably under random-effects models and with attention to prediction intervals, which better convey the likely range of prevalence in comparable future settings [4, 6].

subsections.subsection_title: Prevalence of Intestinal Helminth and Schistosoma mansoni Infections
subsections.content:
Primary studies from Ethiopia indicate marked geographic variation in helminth burden among school-age children. In Medebay Zana woreda, the overall prevalence of intestinal helminth infection was 12.7%, with most infections occurring as single-species infections and Schistosoma mansoni identified as the leading parasite among positive cases; its prevalence was 4.9% in the total sample and 38.5% among infected children ref [20]. This relatively modest overall prevalence contrasts with the persistence of focal transmission in riverine and irrigation-linked settings.

A much higher burden was documented in Sanja town, where overall helminth infection reached 96.6% and S. mansoni alone accounted for 89.9% of examined school children ref [9]. In that study, hookworm (37.1%), Ascaris lumbricoides (16.1%), Hymenolepis nana (8.1%), Taenia species (1.6%), and Trichuris trichiura (0.8%) were also detected, underscoring the frequent overlap between schistosomiasis and other intestinal helminths ref [9]. Comparable surveys from northwest and northern Ethiopia have likewise reported substantial local heterogeneity, ranging from moderate prevalence in some communities to very high endemicity in others ref [3], ref [4], ref [5].

Taken together, these findings show that prevalence estimates for intestinal helminths and S. mansoni in Ethiopian children are highly context-dependent, shaped by ecological exposure, especially proximity to infested water bodies, and by local sanitation conditions. The coexistence of low-prevalence settings such as Medebay Zana and hyperendemic foci such as Sanja highlights why pooled national estimates should be interpreted alongside site-level epidemiology ref [20], ref [9], ref [3], ref [6].

Across Ethiopian studies, Schistosoma mansoni infection in children is consistently patterned by environmental exposure rather than occurring randomly. The strongest determinants are residence or schooling near perennial rivers, streams, irrigation canals, or lakeshores, where contact with cercaria-contaminated water is frequent. Surveys from rural Bahir Dar, Jimma-area riverine schools, and Hayk identified higher odds of infection among children living close to open freshwater bodies and in communities with limited safe water access, indicating that local transmission ecology remains central to infection risk [1, 2, 3].

Behavioral factors further amplify this environmental risk. Recurrent swimming, bathing, washing clothes, crossing rivers barefoot, fishing-related activities, and other routine water-contact practices were repeatedly associated with S. mansoni positivity among school-age children [1, 2, 4]. Male sex and older childhood were also commonly linked with higher prevalence, plausibly reflecting greater mobility and more intense recreational or occupational water exposure. In several settings, poor sanitation and open defecation around water bodies likely sustained contamination of snail habitats, reinforcing transmission cycles [2, 5].

Beyond schistosomiasis-specific exposures, coexisting social and nutritional vulnerabilities appear to shape infection burden. Population-based data from Amhara and studies from western Ethiopia suggest that poverty-related conditions, inadequate hygiene infrastructure, and undernutrition cluster with helminth infection risk and may worsen susceptibility or morbidity [5, 6]. Taken together, the evidence indicates that effective control in Ethiopian children requires chemotherapy to be complemented by safe-water access, sanitation improvement, health education targeting risky water contact, and focal interventions in riverine and irrigation-linked communities [3, 7].

subsections.section_title: Figures and Visual Presentation of Results
subsections.subsection_title: Figures and Visual Presentation of Results
subsections.content:
Visual presentation is central to communicating a meta-analysis of Schistosoma mansoni prevalence in Ethiopian children. A PRISMA-style flow diagram should summarize study identification, screening, eligibility assessment, and final inclusion, thereby making the review process transparent and reproducible, while a summary table can compactly display study location, sample size, diagnostic method, age range, and reported prevalence across settings ref [18], ref [16]. Because Ethiopian studies span diverse ecological zones and transmission contexts, a map of study sites is also valuable for showing geographic clustering and gaps in evidence, complementing national parasitological mapping efforts ref [2], ref [7].

The forest plot remains the primary figure for pooled prevalence, as it simultaneously presents study-specific estimates, confidence intervals, weights, and the overall summary effect. In this topic, where substantial between-study variation is expected across regions, surveys, and diagnostic approaches, the figure should report heterogeneity metrics such as I2 and support subgroup visualization by region, study period, or diagnostic technique ref [19], ref [6]. If enough studies are available, stratified forest plots can make contrasts between high-burden foci and lower-prevalence settings more interpretable than text alone ref [7], ref [11].

Additional figures should address robustness and potential bias. Funnel plots can provide a visual check for small-study effects, although interpretation should be cautious in prevalence meta-analyses with marked heterogeneity; sensitivity plots or leave-one-out displays are often more informative for identifying influential studies. Where diagnostic procedures differ, visual comparison of estimates from single-slide, duplicate-slide, or pooled examination strategies can help readers understand whether observed variation reflects epidemiology, measurement, or both ref [16], ref [6].

The accumulated evidence indicates that Schistosoma mansoni remains a substantial pediatric public health burden in Ethiopia, but one that is highly heterogeneous rather than uniformly distributed. Meta-analytic syntheses place the national burden in a moderate endemicity range, while also showing pronounced between-region and between-study variation, with higher estimates repeatedly observed in southern and some agrarian settings and lower prevalence in more arid or high-altitude areas ref [7], ref [8]. This heterogeneity should therefore be interpreted as epidemiologically meaningful, reflecting ecological suitability, water contact patterns, and unequal exposure rather than mere sampling noise.

Distributional patterns are strongly shaped by geography and local transmission ecologies. Biogeographical synthesis shows endemic sites concentrated across Amhara, Oromia, SNNPR, and Tigray, typically within altitude and temperature bands favorable to Biomphalaria habitats and parasite development ref [8]. Population-based evidence from Amhara further illustrates this focality, with zonal S. mansoni prevalence ranging from below 1% to about 40%, despite a much lower regional average, emphasizing the coexistence of low-risk and hotspot districts within the same region ref [23]. Similar small-area clustering has been reported elsewhere in East Africa, where infection risk intensified around densely populated shoreline environments and modified water systems ref [9].

Risk interpretation in Ethiopian children consistently points to behaviorally mediated freshwater exposure. School- and community-based studies in Amhara and eastern Ethiopia link infection with swimming, bathing, washing, and irrigation-related contact, while also implicating poor knowledge of transmission and prevention as amplifiers of risk ref [24], ref [10]. The gender gradient reported in national synthesis—higher odds among boys—likely reflects differential activity patterns rather than intrinsic susceptibility ref [7]. Comparative evidence from Uganda reinforces that individual open-water sanitation and contact behaviors may be more predictive of infection than household infrastructure alone, underscoring the need to read prevalence maps through a transmission-risk lens rather than as static burden snapshots ref [26].

Taken together, the Ethiopian burden is best understood as a patchwork of persistent micro-endemic foci embedded within broader moderate endemicity. For interpretation, this means that national averages are useful for advocacy, but district- and community-level ecology, child behavior, and water-contact practices are more informative for identifying where the highest pediatric risk is concentrated ref [8], ref [10].

subsections.subsection_title: Programmatic Conclusions From Mapping and Diagnosis
subsections.content:
Programmatic interpretation of Ethiopian mapping data should distinguish tools used for prevalence classification from those suitable for estimating infection intensity. During the national mapping in Amhara, pooling stool samples markedly reduced laboratory time, but substantially lowered sensitivity for detecting S. mansoni, especially in low-intensity settings; thus pooled Kato-Katz may support rapid appraisal of mean intensity but is poorly suited for prevalence-based treatment decisions at baseline or during verification of control progress [1]. This is particularly important in children, among whom light infections can still be epidemiologically meaningful for classifying implementation units.

A second programmatic conclusion concerns diagnostic choice for mapping itself. Accumulating evidence around the point-of-care circulating cathodic antigen (POC-CCA) urine assay indicates that it is operationally attractive for large-scale mapping and often more sensitive than single-sample Kato-Katz for S. mansoni, particularly where infection intensities are light; however, interpretation of trace results and assay standardization remain important for translating test positivity into treatment thresholds [2]. In Ethiopia, this implies that diagnosis-driven maps may vary depending on whether Kato-Katz or antigen detection is used, and that historical prevalence surfaces based on stool microscopy may underestimate residual endemicity in some child populations [2].

Mapping studies from other African programs reinforce the value of geographically explicit diagnosis for preventive chemotherapy planning. In Sierra Leone, district-level and spatially modeled S. mansoni distributions were used directly to stratify annual versus biennial praziquantel delivery, illustrating how prevalence mapping can be converted into operational treatment schedules when linked to WHO thresholds [3]. For Ethiopia, the analogous lesson is that mapping should prioritize sufficient spatial resolution, ecologically informed site selection, and fit-for-purpose diagnostics, because under-detection at baseline risks undertreatment, whereas insensitive follow-up tools may falsely suggest programmatic success [1],[3].

Evidence on treatment support in Ethiopia indicates that both praziquantel performance and delivery coverage must be interpreted together. A recent cross-sectional survey of school-age children showed that praziquantel coverage remains below programmatic expectations in some settings, with uptake shaped by school attendance, drug distribution practices, awareness of mass drug administration, and local implementation factors rather than need alone ref [30]. This is important for S. mansoni control because high-prevalence foci can persist even where preventive chemotherapy is formally adopted if effective coverage is patchy.

At the same time, therapeutic response to praziquantel appears generally favorable. A systematic review and meta-analysis from Ethiopia reported good overall efficacy of praziquantel against S. mansoni in children, supporting its continued use as the backbone of preventive chemotherapy ref [3]. However, the same evidence base suggests that cure rates and egg-reduction outcomes are not uniform across studies, likely reflecting differences in baseline intensity, reinfection pressure, timing of post-treatment assessment, and diagnostic approach ref [3]. In highly exposed communities, therefore, apparent residual positivity after treatment should not automatically be interpreted as drug failure.

Programmatically, these findings support two linked conclusions. First, improving the reach and equity of school-based and community-linked praziquantel delivery is as important as maintaining drug supply ref [30]. Second, impact evaluation should rely on standardized parasitological follow-up and repeated treatment in persistent hotspots, rather than assuming that a single round will durably suppress transmission ref [3]. For Ethiopia, treatment support is therefore best framed not only as access to praziquantel, but as a combination of sufficient coverage, repeated implementation, and realistic interpretation of post-treatment infection patterns.

subsections.subsection_title: Policy, Strategy, and Control Program Support
subsections.content:
From a policy and strategy perspective, the Ethiopian experience shows that schistosomiasis control advanced most rapidly when national leadership, evidence-based planning, and donor coordination were aligned. The Federal Ministry of Health used the national NTD master planning process, dedicated action plans, and a country-led mapping agenda to convert schistosomiasis from a fragmented intervention area into a program with defined geographic targets, phased scale-up, and explicit financing needs ref [32], ref [5].

This is consistent with broader arguments that schistosomiasis elimination cannot rely on drug distribution alone, but requires a long-term, integrated strategy linking preventive chemotherapy with diagnostics, surveillance, health education, snail control, and WASH, supported by sustained political commitment and operational capacity ref [3]. In Ethiopia, the resource-mobilization model was especially important because national mapping data provided a credible basis for partner engagement and helped secure support for nationwide treatment expansion among school-aged children, while also highlighting the need to plan beyond morbidity control toward interruption of transmission ref [32], ref [5].

Accordingly, policy support for S. mansoni control in Ethiopia should prioritize three linked actions: maintaining government ownership of mapping-to-treatment decision pathways; protecting financing continuity beyond short donor cycles; and broadening strategy from school-based deworming to integrated, locally adapted elimination packages in persistent hotspots. Such a framework is more likely to sustain gains, address residual transmission, and align national control efforts with evolving global elimination goals ref [3], ref [5], ref [32].

subsections.subsection_title: Water, Sanitation, and Cross-Cutting Supportive Evidence
subsections.content:
Water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) are highly relevant to interpreting childhood Schistosoma mansoni transmission in Ethiopia because the parasite depends on repeated human contact with infested freshwater and contamination of transmission sites with feces. The strongest cross-cutting synthesis available shows that access to safe water is associated with substantially lower odds of schistosome infection overall, while adequate sanitation is also associated with lower odds of S. mansoni infection; however, the underlying evidence base is dominated by observational studies with considerable heterogeneity and generally modest methodological quality [1].

These findings are consistent with Ethiopian field studies in which river contact, swimming, bathing, washing clothes, and residence near open water repeatedly emerge as major correlates of S. mansoni infection among school-age children, indicating that WASH should be viewed less as a stand-alone intervention and more as a transmission-modifying platform that reduces risky water exposure when combined with chemotherapy and health education [2,3,4]. Evidence from broader integrated NTD programming similarly suggests that improvements in water access, latrine use, and hygiene-related behaviours can accompany declines in helminth transmission, although causal attribution remains difficult in routine program settings [5].

For policy support, the practical implication is not that WASH can replace preventive chemotherapy, but that persistent hotspots in Ethiopia are unlikely to be sustainably controlled without parallel investments in safe domestic water, sanitation coverage, and behaviour change around freshwater contact. At the same time, the WASH-schistosomiasis literature highlights major evidence gaps: poor standardization of water and sanitation measures, limited adjustment for socioeconomic confounding, and scarce community-level analyses. These limitations justify stronger intersectoral surveillance and better-designed implementation research linking school-based infection data with local water infrastructure, sanitation access, and environmental exposure patterns [1,6].
